title: Alterations in Proteomic and Metabolomic Profiles of Cryptococcus neoformans following Hsl101 and Urk1 Deletion
projectDescription: Cryptococcus neoformans is a significant human fungal pathogen, and its kinases, Hsl101 and Urk1, play pivotal roles in virulence during lung and brain infections. This study systematically investigates the effects of Hsl101 and Urk1 deletions on the proteomic and metabolomic profiles of C. neoformans. By generating deletion mutants for Hsl101, we identified profound alterations in the expression levels of 366 proteins and 421 metabolites, including those involved in oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis. Similarly, deletion of Urk1 resulted in significant changes in the expression of 236 proteins and 366 metabolites, highlighting pathways such as steroid biosynthesis and starch and sucrose metabolism. These findings not only elucidate the regulatory roles of Hsl101 and Urk1 in the metabolic pathways of C. neoformans but also pave the way for potential therapeutic interventions targeting these kinases.
sampleProcessingProtocol: To assess the differences in proteomics and metabolomics between wild-type (WT) and mutant strains, cells were cultured overnight in YPD medium at 30°C with continuous shaking at 150 rpm. Following this incubation period, the cells were harvested, washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and the resultant cell pellets were frozen in liquid nitrogen for storage at -80°C. The first step in the proteomic analysis involved extracting proteins from the biological samples. Tissue samples were triturated in liquid nitrogen, and then sonicated in a lysis buffer that contained a variety of reagents. After extraction, centrifugation was carried out to clarify the mixture and isolate the supernatant. Proteins were precipitated using methanol saturated with ammonium sulfate and subjected to multiple washing steps to eliminate contaminants. The concentration of the proteins was precisely measured using a BCA assay. Subsequent to protein quantification, trypsin digestion commenced with protein precipitation through trichloroacetic acid treatment. The precipitated proteins were washed further and then redissolved in triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer. Trypsin was added for overnight digestion to ensure thorough enzymatic hydrolysis, along with reduction and alkylation treatments to promote peptide formation. The resulting peptides underwent desalting in preparation for further analytical procedures. For liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis, the tryptic peptides were resuspended in solvent A and loaded onto a custom-designed reversed-phase analytical column measuring 25 cm in length and 100 μm in inner diameter. The mobile phase comprised two solvents: solvent A contained 0.1% formic acid in 2% acetonitrile in water, while solvent B consisted of 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile. Peptide separation was accomplished using a calibrated gradient: from 0 to 14 minutes, the concentration of solvent B increased from 6% to 24%; from 14 to 16 minutes, it climbed from 24% to 35%; from 16 to 18 minutes, it surged from 35% to 90%; and from 18 to 20 minutes, it was held at 90% solvent B. The flow rate was consistently maintained at 500 nl/min using the Easy-nLC1000 UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics). The separated peptides were directed into a capillary source for analysis on the timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer, applying an electrospray voltage of 1.75 kV to facilitate peptide ionization. The analysis captured both precursor ions and their fragments using the TOF detector, with the timsTOF Pro operating in data-independent parallel accumulation serial fragmentation (dia-PASEF) mode. The full mass spectrometry (MS) scan range was configured from 300 to 1500 m/z, enabling broad detection of ionized peptides, while 20 PASEF-MS/MS scans were gathered per cycle. The MS/MS scans were confined to a range of 400 to 850 m/z, with an isolation window of 7 m/z. The acquired DIA data were subsequently processed using the DIA-NN search engine (version 1.8).
dataProcessingProtocol: Tandem mass spectrometry data were compared against the database for Cryptococcus neoformans var. grubii serotype A strain H99 (C. neoformans var. grubii serotype A strain H99 235443 PR 20240409.fasta), which includes 7,429 entries. To improve the reliability of the findings, this database was supplemented with a reverse decoy database. Trypsin/P was designated as the cleavage enzyme, permitting a maximum of one missed cleavage event. Fixed modifications included the removal of the N-terminal methionine and the carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues. A false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of less than 1% was maintained to ensure a high level of confidence in protein identifications. Bioinformatics analyses played a crucial role in the study. Gene Ontology (GO) terms were utilized to annotate proteins in relation to their cellular components, molecular functions, and biological processes. Additionally, KEGG pathway annotations were applied to link the identified proteins with established biological pathways, offering insights into their functional roles. Specialized software tools were used to predict the subcellular localization of both eukaryotic and prokaryotic proteins. Transcription factors were identified through established databases to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms in play. Functional enrichment analysis was accomplished using Fisher's exact test, with an emphasis on differentially expressed proteins. The proteins identified served as a reference background for this analysis. Significant functional terms were characterized by a fold enrichment greater than 1.5 and a p-value of less than 0.05. Finally, enrichment-based clustering was performed for data visualization through hierarchical clustering, providing a detailed overview of functional classifications and their importance within the analyzed proteomes.
keywords: Cryptococcus neoformans; kinase; hsl101; urk1; proteome; metabolomics
